adults.title: Act Well Thy Part: The Road to Real Happiness
adults.big_idea: In Heavenly Father’s plan, a life of integrity and virtue, kept honest by daily repentance, leads to true happiness and the companionship of the Holy Ghost.
adults.objective: Learners will explain in their own words how integrity, virtue and happiness are linked, and will choose one specific place in their week where they will live more fully what they believe.
prepare: Read Elder Cook’s talk, marking paragraphs T24.04–T24.10 and T24.22–T24.25.
Write on the board: “WHAT-E’ER THOU ART ACT WELL THY PART.”
Bring paper and pens for each person.
Write three group assignments on slips of paper (see segment 3).
Pray for the people you teach by name. Some carry private burdens about honesty, habits or regret; teach with hope.

segments.name: What do we chase?
steps: Begin with prayer. Write the word happiness in the middle of the board.
Ask pairs to take one minute: Where do the people around us look for happiness? Take four or five quick answers and write them around the word.
Read the first key quote aloud (T24.10). Explain that Elder Cook taught that the link between virtue and happiness is not as well understood today as it was in the past.
Tell the class that today they will test that link against their own experience.
questions: When has doing the right thing, even at a cost, left you happier than the easier choice would have?

segments.name: The stone above the door
steps: Point to the inscription on the board. Retell the account briefly: as a new missionary in Scotland, Elder David O. McKay passed a building with these words carved in the stone above the doorway. Elder Cook said the message stayed with him as a missionary and for the rest of his life.
Read the key quote from T24.05 about what he determined to do.
Explain that Elder Cook drew a further lesson: some conduct that is not inherently evil can keep us from spiritual matters that would bless us now and forever.

Give everyone one minute of silent writing: List the parts you hold right now (disciple, spouse, parent, friend, employee, minister, neighbor). Put a star by the one where you most want to do your very best.
Invite two or three to share what they starred, if they wish.
questions: What is something good, or at least harmless, that can quietly crowd out the things that matter most?
What does acting well your part look like when no one is watching?

segments.name: Three small groups, three words
steps: Divide into three groups and hand out the slips. Give them four minutes to read and prepare a one-minute report.

Group 1, integrity: Read Doctrine and Covenants 124:20 and Luke 6:46. Then read President Kimball’s definition of integrity (aligned quote). Report: What does it mean to be someone the Lord can trust?

Group 2, virtue: Read Doctrine and Covenants 121:45–46 and Philippians 4:8. Elder Cook said virtue includes a strong personal moral compass and also cleanliness, modesty, goodness, holiness, and reverence for the sacred. Report: Which of these does our day most need, and why?

Group 3, our words: Elder Cook warned that much conduct and language in society and on social media is coarse and crude, and that we can strive to be a peaceable people. Read Elder Kyungu’s words (aligned quote). Report: What would a peacemaker do differently online and at home this week?
Hear the three reports. After each, ask the whole class the question below.
questions: What would this look like on an ordinary Tuesday?

segments.name: Repentance is part of integrity
steps: Say that a lesson on integrity can leave some of us feeling we fall short. Elder Cook answered that feeling directly. Read the key quote from T24.23.

Retell his missionary experience faithfully: in the British Mission he taught a man who had served on a battleship in the European theater in World War II, 16 years earlier. When the man learned about repentance he was overcome with emotion. He compared it to arriving back in England, leaving the ship, and feeling the earth of his island home under his feet; he had fallen to his knees in appreciation.
Add the detail that just before his baptism the man prayed that he could give others the same joy, and added, “Especially my family.”
Allow a quiet half minute before discussing.
questions: Why is admitting our faults to the Lord an act of integrity rather than a sign that we lack it?
When has repentance felt to you like solid ground under your feet?

segments.name: The reward
steps: Read the key quote from T24.22 about the ultimate reward of integrity and virtue. Remind the class that President McKay taught, as Elder Cook quoted, that happiness is the purpose and design of existence.
Check for understanding: ask each person to turn to a neighbor and finish this sentence in their own words: Integrity and virtue lead to happiness because…
Invite one or two to share what their neighbor said.
questions: How have you noticed the Holy Ghost more when your private life and your beliefs matched?

segments.name: Choose and act
steps: Elder Cook did not give a list of assignments, so invite each person to ask the Lord what to do with what they felt. Show the ideas under Act this week and ask them to write one choice on their paper, next to the part they starred.
Point them to the promise Elder Cook did give: if we dedicate some time every day to the scriptures and spiritual renewal, we will be deeply blessed.

Bear your testimony of the Father’s plan of happiness and of the Savior. Tell the class you will open next week by asking what they noticed. Next week, begin with: Where did you act well your part, and what did you feel?

key_quotes.text: In the Father’s plan, integrity, virtue, and happiness are intrinsically linked.
He determined that whatever responsibility he had, he would do his very best.
Part of having integrity is acknowledging our faults to the Lord and repenting of transgressions.
The ultimate reward of integrity and virtue is the constant companionship of the Holy Ghost.

scriptures.use: Group 1 reads it to see why the Lord said a servant could be trusted; ask what earns that trust today.
Group 1 reads it with D&C 124:20. Ask: Where is the gap between what I say and what I do?
Group 2 reads both verses and lists the blessings promised to those whose thoughts are filled with virtue.
Group 2 reads it as a test for what we watch, read, post and say.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Spencer W. Kimball
aligned_quotes.text: integrity (the willingness and ability to live by our beliefs and commitments) is one of the foundation stones of good character

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Kyungu
aligned_quotes.text: Let us use the language that uplifts, edifies, comforts, and brings people together.

takeaways: Happiness is the fruit of integrity and virtue, not a separate goal.
Whatever part I hold, I can do my very best in it.
Daily repentance is part of integrity and brings the Holy Ghost.
act: Choose one part you starred and do one concrete thing this week to act it well.
Set aside a fixed time each day for the scriptures and spiritual renewal, even ten minutes.
Before you post, reply or speak in frustration, run it past Philippians 4:8.
Each night, tell the Lord honestly about one fault and ask for His help to change.
adapt: At home or with fewer than six people: skip the groups and read the three sets of passages together, one question each.
Large class: form groups by rows and let two groups share each assignment; take only one report per topic.
Short on time: keep segments 2, 4 and 6, and send the group passages home as personal study.

youth.title: Same Person Everywhere
youth.big_idea: Living what we believe, with clean thoughts and words and with daily repentance, is how real happiness and the Holy Ghost come into our lives.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to say what integrity and virtue are in their own words, test their own words and media against Philippians 4:8, and choose one honest change to make this week.
prepare: Read Elder Cook’s talk, especially T24.04–T24.10, T24.15 and T24.22–T24.25.
Write each word of the inscription “WHAT-E’ER THOU ART ACT WELL THY PART” on its own slip of paper; make one mixed-up set for every three or four youth.
Bring paper and pens. Ask youth to have scriptures or the Gospel Library app ready.
Write the three scenarios from segment 3 on cards.

segments.name: Sixty-second happy list
steps: Start the moment they sit down. In teams of three or four, they have 60 seconds to write as many things as they can that people their age say will make them happy.
Count the lists; cheer the longest. Then ask each team to circle the items that still make a person happy a year later.
Say: Elder Quentin L. Cook of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught where lasting happiness comes from. Read the key quote from T24.10. Pray together.
questions: Why do you think so few items got circled?

segments.name: Unscramble the stone
steps: Hand each team a set of word slips. First team to put the seven words in order wins. (They rhyme: art, part.)

Tell the story: as a new missionary in Scotland, Elder David O. McKay, who later became President of the Church, passed a building with this message carved in stone above the doorway. Elder Cook said it influenced him as a missionary and for the rest of his life.
Read the key quote from T24.05.
Have each person write three parts they play right now (for example: friend, teammate, student, sister or brother, quorum or class member, disciple of Jesus Christ).
questions: Put the inscription in your own words. How would you say it to a friend?
Which of your parts is easiest to do halfway?

segments.name: Integrity: three quick scenes
steps: Read President Kimball’s definition of integrity (aligned quote). Ask someone to restate it in ten words or fewer.
On phones or in scriptures, have half the class read Doctrine and Covenants 124:20 and half read Luke 6:46. Each half tells the other what they found.

Give each team one scenario card to act out in under a minute, showing what integrity would look like. These are made-up situations: (1) A group chat starts mocking a classmate and everyone is adding to it. (2) A friend offers you the answers to tonight’s assignment. (3) Someone is one person at church and a different person at practice or online.
After each scene, ask the question below. Keep it honest; do not let anyone make the right choice look easy.
questions: What makes this hard in real life, and what would make it possible?
Why would the Lord care whether He can trust us?

segments.name: The Philippians 4:8 filter
steps: Read the key quote from T24.15. Explain that Elder Cook also taught that the Lord has inspired marvelous technology that blesses us when used wisely. The phone is not the problem; how we use it can be.
Read Philippians 4:8 together. As a class, pull out its tests and list them on the board.
Private phone check, two minutes, no sharing: silently look at your last few messages, comments or posts. Would they pass the tests on the board? Nobody will ask what you found.
Read Elder Kyungu’s words (aligned quote). Ask each team for one specific way to use a phone this week to lift someone.
questions: Elder Cook said virtue includes cleanliness, modesty, goodness, holiness, and reverence for the sacred. Which of those is hardest to keep where you spend time, and what helps?

segments.name: What if I have already blown it?
steps: Say that this is a question many people carry: If I have done things I am not proud of, am I a fake for being here? Let them think before anyone answers.
Read the key quote from T24.23. Point out that, according to Elder Cook, repenting is part of having integrity, not the opposite of it.

Tell his story: as a young missionary in the British Mission he taught a man who had served on a battleship in World War II. When the man learned about repentance he was overcome. He said it felt like the day he came home to England, stepped off the ship, felt the earth of his island home under his feet, and fell to his knees in appreciation.
Elder Cook reminded us that the Savior did not come to condemn the world but to save it. Invite one youth to read John 3:16–17.
Share what Elder Cook called the ultimate reward of integrity and virtue: the constant companionship of the Holy Ghost. Bear a short testimony that the Savior makes coming home possible.
questions: Why is it honest, not hypocritical, to keep coming to church while you are still repenting?
What does it feel like when the Holy Ghost is with you again?

segments.name: One honest change
steps: Check for understanding: each person writes one sentence finishing this thought: Integrity means…  Have three volunteers read theirs.
Show the ideas under Act this week. Each person picks one, or writes a better one, and puts the paper where they will see it.
Share the promise Elder Cook gave: if we dedicate some time every day to the scriptures and spiritual renewal, we will be deeply blessed.
Follow up next week: open by asking, Where were you the same person everywhere this week, and how did it feel?

key_quotes.text: In the Father’s plan, integrity, virtue, and happiness are intrinsically linked.
He determined that whatever responsibility he had, he would do his very best.
Any use of the internet to bully, destroy a reputation, or place a person in a bad light is reprehensible.
Part of having integrity is acknowledging our faults to the Lord and repenting of transgressions.

scriptures.use: Half the class reads it and tells the other half why the Lord said this servant could be trusted.
The other half reads it and explains the gap the Savior is asking about.
Read together; list its tests on the board and use them as a filter for messages, posts and media.
One youth reads both verses aloud after the battleship story; ask what verse 17 says about why the Savior came.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Spencer W. Kimball
aligned_quotes.text: integrity (the willingness and ability to live by our beliefs and commitments) is one of the foundation stones of good character

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Kyungu
aligned_quotes.text: Let us use the language that uplifts, edifies, comforts, and brings people together.

takeaways: Integrity is being the same disciple of Jesus Christ everywhere.
What I think, post and say shapes how happy I am.
Repenting every day is part of integrity, and it brings the Holy Ghost back.
act: Pick one of your parts and do it all the way for seven days.
Run every post, comment and message this week through Philippians 4:8 before you send it.
Send one message a day that lifts somebody.
Spend ten minutes a day in the scriptures, then tell Heavenly Father honestly about one thing you want to change.
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: do the unscramble as a race against a timer, and talk through the scenarios instead of acting them out.
No phones available: skip the private phone check and have each person silently recall the last three things they said about someone who was not present.
Short on time: keep segments 2, 5 and 6.

children.title: Choosing the Right Makes Me Happy
children.big_idea: When I do what is right, I am happy and the Holy Ghost can be with me.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that choosing the right brings happiness, and will name one right thing they will do this week.
prepare: Read Elder Cook’s talk, especially T24.04–T24.05, T24.14 and T24.22.
Draw a large stone shape on gray or plain paper and write on it: Do your very best.
Bring a soft ball, a flashlight, a small blanket or cloth, paper and crayons.
Place a picture of the Savior at the front of the room.
Practice the truth with actions: When I do what is right (thumbs up), I am happy (point to your smile).

segments.name: Welcome and our one truth
steps: Invite a child to pray. Sing “Choose the Right Way” together.
Teach the truth with actions: When I do what is right (thumbs up), I am happy (point to your smile). Say it three times: whisper, normal voice, then standing tall.
Tell the children that Elder Cook, one of the Lord’s Apostles, taught this at general conference.

segments.name: The message on the stone
steps: Hold up the paper stone. Tell the story simply: a long time ago, a new missionary named Elder McKay was in a country called Scotland. He walked past a building and saw words carved in the stone over the door. The words told him to act his part well. He decided that whatever job he had, he would do his very best. Later he became the prophet.
Have the children pretend to walk down a street, stop, look up high, and say with you what he decided: Do your very best.
Pass the stone around the circle. Each child who holds it names something they can do their very best at (being a friend, a helper, a class member, a follower of Jesus).
questions: How do you feel inside when you have done your very best?

segments.name: Happy steps
steps: Line the children up at the back of the room, facing the picture of the Savior.
Read a choice. If it is a right choice, they take one big step forward and say, I am happy. If it is not, they stay still and one child tells what we could do instead; then everyone steps.

Choices: telling the truth when it is hard; saying unkind words to someone; helping clean up without being asked; taking something that is not mine; saying my prayers; using kind words when I feel grumpy; saying sorry when I make a mistake.
When they reach the front, say the truth with actions once more. Then say the first line of the thirteenth article of faith together (Articles of Faith 1:13).
questions: Who helps us choose the right?

segments.name: The flashlight and the blanket
steps: Dim the lights if you can. Shine the flashlight on the wall. Say: when we do what is right, the Holy Ghost can be with us and guide us, like a light.
Cover the flashlight with the blanket. Say: when we choose wrong, it is harder to feel that light.
Ask what we can do. Lift the blanket as you explain: we can tell Heavenly Father we are sorry and try again. That is called repenting, and Jesus makes it possible.
Tell them briefly: Elder Cook taught a man who said repenting felt like the day he came home after being far away on a ship, when he was so glad that he knelt down to say thank you.
Let two or three children take a turn lifting the blanket and saying, I can try again.
questions: How do you feel after you say sorry and try again?

segments.name: Kind words ball
steps: Sit in a circle. Explain that one way to do what is right is to use kind words.
Roll the ball to a child and say something kind to them. That child rolls it to another child and says something kind, until everyone has had a turn.
Ask how the room feels now. Point out that kind words make the giver and the receiver happy.

segments.name: Draw it
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Ask them to draw themselves doing one right thing this week: telling the truth, helping, using kind words, praying.
As they draw, go to each child and ask them to tell you about the picture. Write their words at the bottom if they wish.
Invite a few to show their drawing and say: I will ___, and I will be happy.

segments.name: Testimony and sending home
steps: Say the truth with actions one last time. This is your check: can every child say it without you?
Bear a short testimony that Heavenly Father loves them and sent His Son, Jesus Christ, and that the Lord wants us to feel the joy of doing right.
Ask them to put the drawing where they will see it at home. Tell them that next week you will ask what right thing they did and how they felt. Next week, begin by asking exactly that.

key_quotes.text: He determined that whatever responsibility he had, he would do his very best.
The Lord wants us to experience the joy of a virtuous life.
But when we do what is right, He can dwell with us and guide us in all that we do.

scriptures.use: Tell the children in your own words that Heavenly Father loves us so much that He sent Jesus; older children can read the verse aloud during the testimony.
An older child reads it before the drawing; ask the class to listen for words that describe good things to think about.
Say the first line together at the end of Happy steps as a reminder of what we believe.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President David O. McKay
aligned_quotes.text: Virtue, uprightness, faithfulness, holiness, and keeping the commandments of God lead to a happy life.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Kyungu
aligned_quotes.text: let us use words that encourage understanding and peace

takeaways: When I do what is right, I am happy.
The Holy Ghost can be with me when I choose the right.
If I make a mistake, I can say sorry and try again because of Jesus.
act: Do the right thing you drew, and tell someone at home how it felt.
Use kind words every day this week.
Do your very best at one job at home or at school.
When you make a mistake, tell Heavenly Father you are sorry in your prayer and try again.
music: I'm Trying to Be like Jesus

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: shorten the story to three sentences and act it out twice. Use only four choices in Happy steps and let a helper model each one. Repeat the truth with actions after every activity. In the ball game, help each child with a simple phrase such as, You are my friend. Accept scribbles in the drawing and ask the child to tell you about it.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: have one child read Philippians 4:8 aloud and another read the key quote from T24.05. Let an older child lead Happy steps by making up the choices. Ask a harder question: Why is it sometimes hard to tell the truth, and what helps you do it anyway? Share President McKay’s words (aligned quote) and ask which word in his list they want to work on.
